n: Isaiah describes his call as a prophet. In the year King Uzziah died (around 740 BC), Isaiah saw the Lord enthroned in glory, His robe filling the temple. John later says Isaiah saw the glory of Jesus (John 12:41); Nephi testifies that Isaiah saw the Redeemer.

f.g: The hem or flowing skirts of a royal robe.

n: Above Him stood seraphim, each with six wings: two to cover their faces in reverence, two to cover their feet in humility, and two to fly in service.

f.g: “Burning ones” — heavenly beings in God’s presence. (Seraphim is already plural; the KJV adds an extra -s.)

n: The seraphim call to each other, “Holy, holy, holy” — the strongest way in Hebrew to say God is supremely holy. His glory fills the whole earth.

f.w: the whole earth is full of his glory

n: The doorframes shook at their voices and the temple filled with smoke — signs of God’s presence, as at Mount Sinai.
Overwhelmed, Isaiah cries out that he is ruined. Seeing God’s holiness makes him painfully aware of his own sins and his people’s.

f.g: Lips stained by sin — fitting for a man called to speak God’s word.

f.w: mine eyes have seen the King

n: One of the seraphim flies to him holding a burning coal taken from the temple altar with tongs.

f.g: A glowing ember from the altar where sacrifices were offered.

n: The seraph touches Isaiah’s lips with the coal and declares his guilt removed and his sin forgiven. The coal from the altar of sacrifice points to cleansing through the Savior’s Atonement.
Now cleansed, Isaiah hears the Lord ask who will go as His messenger. Isaiah volunteers immediately: “Here am I; send me” — echoing the premortal Savior’s words in the Council in Heaven.

God warns Isaiah that many will hear but not understand, see but not perceive. Jesus quoted this to explain why He taught in parables. 2 Nephi 16:9 reads “but they understood not … but they perceived not,” describing the people rather than commanding them.

f.w: Hear ye indeed, but understand not

n: This is ironic: Isaiah’s preaching will make hard hearts harder, because the people refuse to listen. God isn’t wishing them unhealed; He is describing what rejection of His word will do.

f.w: Make the heart of this people fat

n: Isaiah asks how long this will last. The answer: until the cities are ruined and the land desolate — fulfilled in the Assyrian and Babylonian conquests.
The people will be carried far away into exile, and the land left largely abandoned.
Yet a tenth will remain. Like a felled tree whose stump still lives, Israel will be cut down, but a “holy seed” — a righteous remnant — will sprout again.

f.g: A terebinth, a large tree that can sprout again from its stump.
